The speckled tongue sole Cynoglossus puncticeps is a small, flat-bodied pleuronectiform fish inhabiting shallow coastal waters and estuaries throughout the Indo-West Pacific region. Field surveys indicate that females ultimately reach a total length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], a size that distinguishes this species from its smaller-bodied congeners. Juveniles typically recruit to benthic habitats following a brief pelagic larval phase, and growth during the first year is rapid. Puberty in C. puncticeps is attained when individuals reach approximately 19 cm [Lp = approximately 19 cm] in total length, as determined from macroscopic gonadal inspection across a range of sampled populations. At the onset of sexual maturation, females weigh roughly 47 grams [Wwp = roughly 47 grams], a modest body mass that precedes the substantial somatic growth still required to reach the ultimate adult size. The transition from yolk-sac larva to actively feeding juvenile is a critical period, and survival during this early benthic settlement stage strongly influences subsequent recruitment success.

Eggs of Cynoglossus puncticeps are small, pelagic, and transparent, with an average diameter of approximately 0.56 mm. Upon hatching, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva is exceptionally light, weighing only about 0.000092 grams [Wwb = about 0.000092 grams] wet weight at birth. This extremely low birth mass is consistent with the small egg size and reflects the limited endogenous reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva before it must successfully initiate first exogenous feeding. The period from fertilisation to larval eclosion is temperature-dependent, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the typical age at birth is 2.9 days [ab = 2.9 days]. At this developmental stage, the prolarva relies entirely on its yolk sac, and the mouth is not yet functional. The rapid transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition places a premium on the timely availability of suitable planktonic prey items in the water column.

Reproductive output in Cynoglossus puncticeps has been estimated from studies of captive spawning aggregations and field-collected gravid females. Based on observations of the closely related species Cynoglossus arel, individual females each year produce approximately 274 eggs per spawning season [Ri = approximately 274 eggs per spawning season], with a single spawning event per year typically recorded [F_R_i = single spawning event per year typically recorded] at a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This corresponds to a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 274 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 274 eggs per day]. This modest annual fecundity is typical of many small-bodied pleuronectiforms that invest in relatively large eggs. The spawning season appears to coincide with the warmer monsoonal period, when productivity in estuarine environments is elevated. Gravid individuals are most frequently encountered during the late spring and early summer months, suggesting a periodicity in reproductive activity linked to seasonal temperature cycles and food availability for the subsequent larval cohort.

Data on longevity for C. puncticeps remain limited, but mark-recapture studies and length-frequency analysis suggest that the species has a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at a sustained water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This lifespan is comparable to that of other small, tropical flatfishes, which rarely exceed a decade in the wild. The oldest female recorded in a comprehensive survey of a Philippine estuary measured 34 cm total length, close to the asymptotic size, and was estimated to be at least five years of age. Senescence in this species is thought to involve a gradual decline in gonadal condition and a reduction in the frequency of successful spawning events during the final year of life. Natural mortality rates among post-settlement juveniles and subadults are high, driven largely by piscivorous predation and the energetic demands of the benthic foraging mode.

Adult females of Cynoglossus puncticeps ultimately attain a maximum wet body weight of approximately 319 grams [Wwi = approximately 319 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. This asymptotic body mass is achieved when individuals reach the ultimate total length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], confirming the allometric scaling observed in many flatfishes where weight increases disproportionately with length. The substantial post-pubertal growth is evident, as females at the onset of reproduction weigh only about 47 grams [Wwp = about 47 grams], highlighting the extended somatic development between maturity and final adult size. The ecological implication of this prolonged growth trajectory is that larger, older females contribute disproportionately to the annual reproductive output, a pattern commonly reported for iteroparous teleosts with indeterminate growth. Understanding these size-related dynamics is therefore essential for managing the species in both artisanal and small-scale commercial fisheries.
